chunks: And from him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Abdullah, the two sons of Muhammad ibn Isa, from Dawud al-Sarri, who said:

I was with Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), the third Imam, one day. He sat and spoke until the sun set. Then he called for a candle while still sitting and speaking. When I left the house, I looked and saw that the twilight (shafaq) had disappeared before he prayed Maghrib. Then he called for water, performed ablution, and prayed.

Therefore, these narrations are to be understood as being in a state of necessity (darurah), because with necessity, it is permissible to delay the prayer from its initial time — and that which indicates this.

key_terms.أَوَّلِ وَقْتِهَا: The initial time of the prayer
key_terms.الشَّفَقُ: Twilight, the reddish glow in the sky after sunset
key_terms.الضَّرُورَةِ: Necessity or need, a legal state allowing for flexibility in ritual obligations

ai.seo_question: How do Shia scholars explain delayed prayers in hadith when the time for prayer has seemingly passed?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the practical application of *darurah* (necessity) in Shia jurisprudence, where Imam al-Sadiq (AS) prayed Maghrib after the disappearance of twilight (*shafaq*), deviating from the standard early timing. Scholars interpret this not as a rejection of the preferred time (*awwal al-waqt*), but as evidence that necessity justifies delaying the prayer until the end of its time, a principle derived from the flexibility granted in the Quranic verse 'Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity' (2:286).
